task.goal: Determine whether a classroom light meter's apparent afternoon drift is due to the meter, changing daylight or placement.
hard_constraints: One meter, two rooms, five school days and no electrical modifications.
Measurements cannot interrupt lessons; log time, orientation and weather proxy.
Allow inconclusive findings and state what a control comparison can and cannot establish.
task.available_resources: Window shade, fixed lamp and written observation sheets.

DIRECT_FULL.title: Repeated fixed-lamp reference checks
DIRECT_FULL.proposal:
Primary mechanism: compare classroom readings with a repeatable lamp reference each morning and afternoon. A time-dependent change under approximately constant illumination supports a meter-related explanation; stable reference readings with changing classroom readings support an environmental explanation.

Use one room for the reference station. Close its shade and place the meter at a recorded position, distance and orientation relative to the fixed lamp. Keep the lamp stationary, use its normal switch and power supply, and allow the same warm-up interval before each reference check. Make no electrical modifications. Keep the sensor away from hot surfaces and walking routes.

Across five school days, take brief reference–classroom–reference sequences during existing morning and afternoon breaks. Include the same designated location in each of the two rooms, reversing room order on alternate days. On written sheets record every reading, time, room, sensor orientation, shade and lamp state, weather proxy such as sunny/cloudy, and direct-sun or observer-shadow conditions. Repeat each reading once without moving the sensor.

The main assumptions are repeatable positioning and sufficiently stable lamp output. Shade closure does not guarantee darkness: reference readings still contain daylight. Where practical, record lamp-off and lamp-on readings close together; their difference estimates the lamp contribution if daylight remains stable. No additional equipment is required.

A reference trend cannot independently prove meter drift because lamp output, temperature and residual daylight may also change. A stable reference cannot rule out a meter fault restricted to other brightness levels or light spectra. Report mixed or inconclusive findings when these limitations dominate.
DIRECT_FULL.experiment: During the first available break, repeat the unchanged reference setup, then remove and replace the meter and repeat it again. Compare this repeatability range with subsequent morning–afternoon changes. Also compare lamp-on minus lamp-off differences across the day. If those differences change as much as classroom readings, the reference does not isolate daylight reliably; retain meter-versus-lamp uncertainty rather than assigning a cause.

DIRECT_FULL.title: Rapid shade crossover to isolate daylight contribution
DIRECT_FULL.proposal:
Primary mechanism: deliberately change daylight admission while holding meter placement constant. If afternoon changes substantially weaken when the shade is closed, daylight is implicated through a controlled environmental intervention.

Choose one accessible measurement location in each room and record its position and sensor orientation precisely. During existing morning and afternoon breaks on all five days, take an open–closed–open shade sequence at each location, allowing readings to settle after each change. Reverse the sequence on alternate days to expose order effects. Keep the fixed lamp in one documented state throughout each sequence; if it cannot illuminate both rooms without relocation, leave it unused and keep other controllable lighting unchanged. Restore the shade afterward. Alternate which room is visited first, and avoid moving furniture or interrupting lessons.

Log each reading and its time, orientation, weather proxy, shade state, lighting state, direct sunlight and nearby shadows on written sheets. Compare morning–afternoon changes separately for open and closed conditions within each room. Compare the immediate open-versus-closed effect with the apparent daily drift, rather than assuming equal illumination between rooms.

This requires permission to operate the shades during breaks and enough daylight suppression to produce an informative contrast. Rapid sequences assume illumination does not change substantially between paired measurements; bracket readings help detect violations.

A reproducible shade effect establishes sensitivity to admitted daylight, not perfect meter accuracy. Closed-shade readings may still vary with daylight, and a meter gain error can affect both conditions. A weak shade effect therefore cannot establish meter drift. The two rooms provide replication under different surroundings, not simultaneous controls, because only one meter is available.
DIRECT_FULL.experiment: First compare two consecutive open-shade readings with an open–closed–open sequence at the same location. If closure produces no reproducible change beyond ordinary repetition, this intervention has little discriminatory power there. If the two bracketing open readings differ markedly, flag the sequence as environmentally unstable. Over five days, test whether the afternoon change consistently shrinks with the shade closed; otherwise report daylight attribution as unsupported or incomplete.

DIRECT_FULL.title: Placement crossover with return-to-position checks
DIRECT_FULL.proposal:
Primary mechanism: exchange sensor position and orientation within short measurement blocks to determine whether placement can reproduce the apparent afternoon drift. Returning to the starting configuration separates reproducible placement effects from changes occurring while measurements are taken.

In each room, define configuration A as the usual measurement position and orientation. Define B by changing position while retaining A's orientation, and C by changing orientation at A's position. Use existing desk edges and room features as written location references; do not move furniture. Choose configurations that are safe, accessible during normal breaks and representative of plausible placement differences.

On each of five days, run brief A–B–A and A–C–A blocks during morning and afternoon breaks in both rooms. Alternate the order of the two blocks and the order of room visits across days. Keep shade and lighting states unchanged within each block. Record time, configuration, sensor orientation, weather proxy, direct sunlight and observer shadows for every reading. Keep the observer clear of the sensor's view. Use the fixed lamp, if useful, as a stationary lighting condition in its existing room; no rewiring is needed.

Compare B and C with their surrounding A readings. Then compare morning and afternoon readings taken strictly in configuration A. Repeatable B or C effects show how placement could change the result; persistence of afternoon change at A shows that placement alone is insufficient.

The method assumes configurations can be reproduced and daylight remains sufficiently stable during each short block. It needs only the meter and observation sheets. Orientation sensitivity may reflect normal illumination geometry or imperfect meter response. Without a stable independent reference, residual change cannot be uniquely divided between daylight and meter drift.
DIRECT_FULL.experiment: Begin with A–A–A readings without deliberate movement, then perform one A–B–A and one A–C–A block. A placement effect is credible only if it exceeds ordinary repetition and the return readings approximately agree. Across five days, check whether standardizing A reduces the afternoon pattern compared with the usual-placement observations. If not, placement is not a sufficient explanation; if return readings fail, label the block unstable rather than attributing its differences to placement.

DIRECT_FULL.title: Power-cycle intervention with matched sham checks
DIRECT_FULL.proposal:
Main mechanism: intervene on the meter’s operating history while leaving illumination and placement unchanged. If an afternoon offset repeatedly changes after a normal power cycle, beyond changes during an equally long uninterrupted comparison, that supports an operating-state effect in the meter. Daylight or placement should not respond directly to switching the meter off and on.

This requires a meter with an ordinary accessible power switch and a restart procedure that preserves its measurement mode and range. Follow any manufacturer settling guidance. Use only normal controls; make no electrical modifications. If restarting changes settings that cannot be restored reliably, this approach is unsuitable.

During existing morning and afternoon breaks on five school days, place the meter at one precisely documented location and orientation in each room. Keep shade and lighting states fixed within each block. Take two baseline readings. In a reset block, switch the meter off briefly without moving it, restart, wait the prescribed settling time, and take two further readings. In a sham block, leave it running for the same interval before taking the final readings. Predetermine a balanced schedule so each room receives both interventions in morning and afternoon sessions; alternate room order. If switch operation moves the sensor, flag the block as confounded.

Use the fixed lamp in its existing room, with consistent warm-up and the shade closed, to reduce illumination variability there. The other room tests whether any reset response also occurs under ordinary daylight. Record every reading, time, orientation, weather proxy, lighting and shade state, intervention, restart delay, and any shadows or movement on observation sheets.

A reproducible reset response supports a reset-sensitive meter effect, but does not establish calibration accuracy or exclude simultaneous daylight changes. No response cannot exclude meter drift that survives restarting. Sequential room comparisons cannot provide simultaneous daylight control.
DIRECT_FULL.experiment: First inspect whether the switch can be operated without shifting the sensor or changing settings. Then compare one reset block with one equal-duration sham block under the stationary lamp. A transient restart jump that disappears after settling falsifies treating that jump as persistent drift. Across five days, compare settled before–after changes for reset and sham blocks separately by room and time of day. If reset changes do not consistently exceed ordinary repetition and sham changes, report the intervention as inconclusive rather than assigning the afternoon pattern to the meter.

DIRECT_FULL.title: Blocked-sensor zero checks for additive meter drift
DIRECT_FULL.proposal:
Main mechanism: remove incident light temporarily and inspect whether the meter’s zero reading changes from morning to afternoon. An increasing reading with a reliably blocked sensor supports an additive meter offset, which could contribute to apparent afternoon drift. Daylight and sensor orientation should have little effect when light is adequately excluded. This differs from assuming that a lamp maintains constant output.

The prerequisite is a safe, repeatable way to block light using an accessible section of the available window shade. Use it only if its material can cover the sensor without pulling on fittings, pressing on the sensing surface or risking damage. Do not detach the shade. If the material transmits appreciable light or cannot cover the sensor safely, this alternative is unsuitable.

During existing morning and afternoon breaks over five school days, measure at one documented position and orientation in each room. Take two exposed readings, two blocked readings after the display settles, and two further exposed readings. Alternate room order across days. Keep lighting and shade position unchanged within each block except for the local covering needed for the zero check. Restore everything afterward and make no electrical modifications.

Record readings, times, room, orientation, weather proxy, lighting state, covering arrangement and any movement or shadows on written sheets. Compare morning–afternoon changes in blocked readings with changes in exposed readings. A similar absolute increase would support an additive offset contribution, assuming the blocked condition is valid and the meter uses comparable settings.

A stable zero cannot exclude gain drift, spectral errors or faults occurring only at higher illumination. A changing zero does not establish that the entire classroom change is instrumental. Residual exposed changes can still reflect daylight or placement; this method may therefore produce a partial or inconclusive attribution.
DIRECT_FULL.experiment: At the first break, compare blocked readings with the fixed lamp normally switched off and on, keeping the covering unchanged and allowing readings to settle. Repeat after removing and replacing the covering. A reproducible lamp-dependent change or poor replacement repeatability undermines the dark control. Passing this check only establishes adequate blocking for that tested illumination. Across five days, compare blocked morning–afternoon differences with immediate repeat variation. If blocked readings stay stable while exposed readings change, reject additive zero drift as a sufficient explanation, while retaining other meter faults and environmental causes.

EXPAND.title: Dark-condition checks for an additive meter offset
EXPAND.proposal:
Main mechanism: test whether the meter reports an afternoon increase when essentially no light reaches its sensor. An additive electronic offset can persist in darkness; changing classroom daylight and ordinary sensor placement should not affect a genuinely light-tight reading. This specifically tests one type of meter fault, rather than all possible drift.

During existing morning and afternoon breaks on five school days, take readings at one documented, repeatable location in each room. Then temporarily shield the sensor using several overlapping observation sheets, without pressing on it or covering ventilation openings. Use the same shielding arrangement each time, resting it safely on an existing surface. If the meter design makes shielding unsafe or prevents reading the display, this alternative is unsuitable. No electrical modifications are needed.

Log the time, room, sensor orientation, weather proxy, ordinary reading, shielded reading, lighting conditions and shielding arrangement. Repeat shielded readings after removing and replacing the sheets. Record displayed negative values or error messages rather than treating them as zero. Keep the meter's normal measurement settings unchanged.

Compare morning–afternoon changes in shielded readings with changes in ordinary readings. A repeatable shielded increase supports an additive-offset explanation, provided light leakage has been excluded. Stable shielded readings weaken that explanation but cannot exclude gain drift, spectral sensitivity problems or brightness-dependent faults. They also cannot decide between daylight and placement as causes of ordinary readings. Automatic zero clamping could conceal a real offset; consult any already available operating instructions before interpreting a displayed zero.

The resources are the meter, sheets and safe existing surfaces. The essential uncertainties are whether the improvised shield is sufficiently opaque and whether the display exposes small offsets.
EXPAND.experiment: At the first break, compare the shielded reading under two different external lighting conditions, then add another layer of sheets. If either change shifts the result beyond repeated-reading variation, shielding is inadequate and subsequent dark comparisons are inconclusive. If shielding passes, compare five days of morning and afternoon shielded readings against the simple comparator of an unchanged zero baseline. Attribute only the supported additive component, not the entire classroom change.

EXPAND.title: Vary operating time to test meter warm-up
EXPAND.proposal:
Main mechanism: separate time of day from time since the meter was switched on. If apparent afternoon drift comes from meter warm-up or operating history, changing the start time should change the pattern. Daylight follows outdoor conditions rather than the meter's power-on schedule.

This requires a meter with an ordinary user power switch, permission to leave it operating between breaks, and enough battery capacity. Do not open the meter, change its electrical connections or override automatic shutdown. If its operating duration cannot be controlled or documented, this plan is unsuitable.

Across five school days, alternate two schedules: three days with the meter started shortly before each measurement visit, and two days with it started a substantially longer, documented interval beforehand. Use intervals permitted by its normal operation. Keep storage location and handling consistent, away from direct sun and heat. During existing morning and afternoon breaks, measure the same written position and orientation in both rooms, alternating room order across days. Keep the fixed lamp in its usual location and a consistent operating state; the shade may help reduce daylight variability at a designated comparison location.

Record every reading's time, orientation, weather proxy, room, lighting and shade state, time since power-on, and any shutdown or setting reset. Take two readings without repositioning. Compare morning–afternoon changes under the two operating schedules, and inspect whether readings associate more consistently with elapsed operating time than with afternoon timing.

A repeatable schedule effect supports an instrument-state contribution. It does not prove defective calibration: normal stabilization, temperature or power-cycle setting changes could explain it. Five days provide limited replication, and weather can accidentally align with the schedules. Stable results across schedules cannot exclude other meter faults. Residual classroom changes remain potentially attributable to daylight or placement.
EXPAND.experiment: Before committing the five-day schedule, use one break for a stationary comparison: record readings immediately after normal power-on and at several short intervals, without moving the sensor. Compare any trend with two consecutive readings after the meter has stabilized. Repeat this check during another break. If the early trend is absent or inconsistent, warm-up has little demonstrated explanatory power. If present, test whether longer advance operation reduces the afternoon pattern; inconsistent weather or lamp conditions require an inconclusive finding.

EXPAND.title: Exposure-history crossover to detect meter memory
EXPAND.proposal:
Main mechanism: change the light reaching the meter immediately before measuring the same target. Some meters settle slowly after a large illumination change or retain a temporary effect from overload or automatic range switching. Such exposure history could produce an apparent afternoon drift if afternoon handling exposes the sensor to brighter light. The distinguishing intervention is prior illumination, with position and operating duration held approximately constant.

During existing morning and afternoon breaks across five school days, use one reproducible target position and orientation in each room. Record locations using existing desk edges or other fixed features. Keep shade and lighting states unchanged during each measurement block. In the room containing the fixed lamp, define two safe conditioning positions: one illuminated by the lamp and one shaded from it. Use ordinary indoor light levels, avoid hot surfaces, and never aim at the sun. In the other room, use existing brighter and shaded locations if available; otherwise perform only the standardized target measurements there.

Before each target reading, hold the sensor at one conditioning position for a fixed short interval, then return it to the target. Record the target reading immediately and again after a fixed settling interval. Repeat after the other conditioning position, reversing order across sessions. Keep the meter powered consistently throughout each block. Log time, orientation, weather proxy, conditioning sequence, lighting and shade states, visible shadows and readings on observation sheets.

This requires a meaningful safe illumination contrast and a display fast enough to observe settling. No additional equipment or electrical modifications are needed. A repeatable exposure-history effect supports an instrument-response contribution, but does not establish defective calibration. It explains the original afternoon pattern only if ordinary afternoon handling plausibly creates that history. Stable results cannot exclude other meter faults, and target readings can still change through daylight or imperfect repositioning.
EXPAND.experiment: First compare a bright-conditioned and shaded-conditioned return with a target-to-target control: lift and replace the meter without deliberately changing its illumination. Repeat in reversed order. An exposure-history explanation predicts a larger, reproducible initial difference after different conditioning that diminishes with settling. Comparable differences in the simple replacement control, unstable daylight, or failure to reproduce the effect weaken that explanation. Across five days, inspect whether standardized, settled target readings still show afternoon change; persistence leaves daylight, placement and other meter effects unresolved.
